data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism grounds the preference for corroborated theories in verisimilitude: 'we prefer the theory that has withstood the most severe tests because it is currently the best approximation to the truth (highest verisimilitude).' This is self-undermining under Popper's own framework. Popper accepts that all surviving scientific theories are strictly false. His formal definition of verisimilitude (comparing theories via truth-content minus falsity-content) was proven defective by Miller (1976) and Tichý (1974): under Popper's own definition, no false theory can be shown to have greater verisimilitude than another false theory—the comparative ordering collapses for any pair of false theories. Since the target must rank among false competitors (Popper denies we possess true theories), the claim that one surviving theory has 'highest verisimilitude' among its competitors is formally empty on Popper's own terms. The target's countercondition guards against verisimilitude 'not being definable without probabilistic assumptions,' but the actual defect is different and more fundamental: Popper's verisimilitude IS defined non-probabilistically, yet that very definition fails to do the comparative work the target requires of it. The pragmatic decision rule thus rests on a metric that, in the domain where it is needed (ranking false theories), yields no determinate ordering at all.
